properties.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
properties.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

# Manifest

Manifest is a Technology, Information and Internet company. ManifestIT is a change observability platform that helps intelligently evaluate risk, quantify impact, and break down silos between tools and teams. Manifest employs 24 people. Headquartered in Menlo Park, California, United States. Its workforce is distributed across India, United States, and Canada.

## About

Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has l

properties.name: Manifest
properties.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

entity.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
entity.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

entity.name: Parlon
entity.description:
74% of network teams are actively considering replacing a core management tool. The reason is straightforward: the tools they depend on were built for infrastructure that no longer exists.

Parlon is an infrastructure observability platform purpose-built for hybrid, cloud-native, and AI-driven environments. We unify telemetry from infrastructure, applications, and AI/LLM workflows into a single normalized fabric, giving teams trusted, actionable intelligence before issues reach users or revenue.

Three capabilities set Parlon apart:

Normalization as a Primitive | Parlon normalizes telemetry at ingestion, not after the fact. Every metric lands in a consistent, query-ready model. This structural advantage makes correlation, alerting, and AI-ready analytics dramatically more reliable and eliminates the brittle custom parsers teams shouldn't have to maintain.

LLM-Aware Synthetic Testing | AI workloads introduce failure modes legacy tools were never designed to see. Parlon actively tests AI workflows, monitoring inference latency, response quality, and behavioral drift, while simultaneously observing the underlying infrastructure those workflows depend on. No other platform connects these two layers in a single view.

Alert Auto-Tune™ | Learning-based alerting that continuously adapts to real system behavior, de-duplicates noise, and surfaces what's actually worth acting on. The result is ~70% reduction in alert noise. When Parlon alerts, it earns attention.

Founded by operators with decades inside enterprise observability. Built from first principles for what infrastructure looks like today and where AI is taking it next.

Parlon. Observability for Intelligent Infrastructure. Clean. Fast. Deeply Integrable.

entity.name: Manifest
entity.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

messages.content:
You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

messages.content:
You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).
  List the SEED capabilities this candidate also does, copying the strings
  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

STEP 3 - relevant.
  relevant = anchor_match AND capabilities_matched is non-empty.
  Nothing else changes it.

Rules that apply throughout:
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. A smaller, larger, or
    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).
  List the SEED capabilities this candidate also does, copying the strings
  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

STEP 3 - relevant.
  relevant = anchor_match AND capabilities_matched is non-empty.
  Nothing else changes it.

Rules that apply throughout:
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. A smaller, larger, or
    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

Worked examples (SEED anchor -> candidate -> verdict):
  - "restaurant point-of-sale platform" [payments, online ordering, payroll]
      • a restaurant POS suite with payments and online ordering
        -> anchor true, matched [payments, online ordering], relevant true.
      • a restaurant POS with none of the listed capabilities
        -> anchor true, matched [], relevant FALSE (no overlap).
      • a retail-only POS with payments
        -> anchor FALSE (different customer), relevant false.
      • a general payments processor with no restaurant POS product
        -> anchor FALSE (different category), relevant false.
      • an actual restaurant chain
        -> anchor FALSE (customer of the category), relevant false.
      • an agency that installs restaurant POS systems
        -> anchor FALSE (serves the category), relevant false.
  - "CRM and marketing automation platform for go-to-market teams"
      • a smaller CRM with marketing automation -> anchor true, relevant true.
      • a lead-generation agency using that CRM for clients -> anchor false.
  - "digital bank for consumers"
      • a digital bank in another country -> anchor true (geography is not a
        constraint), relevant true if any capability overlaps.
  - "developer-security platform"
      • a company on a similar cloud stack selling HR software -> anchor false.

  CAPABILITIES (match any subset):

    - log management
    - security monitoring
    - synthetic monitoring

                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

  this company to be in the same market?

                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).

      entries fail.

  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

messages.content:
You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).
    - Parent/holding companies, the seed itself, and duplicate or parody
      entries fail.
  When you cannot tell what the candidate sells, anchor_match is false.

STEP 2 - capabilities_matched (the overlap).
  List the SEED capabilities this candidate also does, copying the strings
  verbatim from the SEED's list. Include a capability when the candidate
  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

STEP 3 - relevant.
  relevant = anchor_match AND capabilities_matched is non-empty.
  Nothing else changes it.

Rules that apply throughout:
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. A smaller, larger, or
    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.

Worked examples (SEED anchor -> candidate -> verdict):
  - "restaurant point-of-sale platform" [payments, online ordering, payroll]
      • a restaurant POS suite with payments and online ordering
        -> anchor true, matched [payments, online ordering], relevant true.
      • a restaurant POS with none of the listed capabilities
        -> anchor true, matched [], relevant FALSE (no overlap).
      • a retail-only POS with payments
        -> anchor FALSE (different customer), relevant false.
      • a general payments processor with no restaurant POS product
        -> anchor FALSE (different category), relevant false.
      • an actual restaurant chain
        -> anchor FALSE (customer of the category), relevant false.
      • an agency that installs restaurant POS systems
        -> anchor FALSE (serves the category), relevant false.
  - "CRM and marketing automation platform for go-to-market teams"
      • a smaller CRM with marketing automation -> anchor true, relevant true.
      • a lead-generation agency using that CRM for clients -> anchor false.
  - "digital bank for consumers"
      • a digital bank in another country -> anchor true (geography is not a
        constraint), relevant true if any capability overlaps.
  - "developer-security platform"
      • a company on a similar cloud stack selling HR software -> anchor false.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it. Resemblance has two halves, and they are judged
DIFFERENTLY:

  ANCHOR       - who the seed sells to, and what it fundamentally is
                 (e.g. "restaurant point-of-sale platform"). This is a HARD
                 requirement. Every lookalike must be the same kind of company
                 for the same kind of customer. No amount of feature overlap
                 substitutes for it.
  CAPABILITIES - what the seed does (e.g. payments, online ordering, payroll,
                 operations). A lookalike matches ANY non-empty subset. It does
                 not need all of them, and matching more is not required to
                 qualify - only to be a closer match.

So: a true lookalike clears the ANCHOR and shares at least one CAPABILITY.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from, with its
    ANCHOR and its CAPABILITIES listed separately.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide in this order, and do not work backwards from a conclusion:

STEP 1 - anchor_match (the gate).
  True only if the CANDIDATE is the same kind of company as the ANCHOR, for
  the same kind of customer. Ask: would someone shopping for the SEED consider
  this company to be in the same market?
    - A different customer fails, even in the same product category
      (restaurant POS vs retail-only POS: the customer differs).
    - A different category fails, even for the same customer
      (a restaurant POS vs a restaurant-supply distributor: both sell to
      restaurants, but only one is the same kind of company).
    - Serving the category rather than competing in it fails: agencies,
      consultancies, integrators, resellers.
    - Being a customer of the category fails (an actual restaurant is not a
      lookalike of a restaurant POS platform).

      entries fail.

  plausibly offers it as part of its product; leave it out when you have no
  evidence. Matching a subset is normal and expected.

  Nothing else changes it.

    differently-located company clears the anchor if it is the same kind of
    company for the same kind of customer. Ignore such metadata.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not an anchor match. Neither
    is a similar technology stack - tech co-signals may support a judgement but
    never establish one.
  - Judge the candidate's primary business, not a side feature.
  - When in doubt on the anchor, answer false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words: name the anchor verdict and the overlap.
